title: Sikh Restaurateur Vows to Sue Met Police Over 'False Arrest'
excerpt: Harman Singh Kapoor, owner of London's Rangrez, accuses Met Police and Mayor Sadiq Khan of discrimination after halal dispute arrest
body:
Harman Singh Kapoor, the Sikh owner of Rangrez restaurant in Hammersmith, west London, announced plans to pursue legal action against the Metropolitan Police and Mayor Sadiq Khan following what he calls a discriminatory false arrest on March 14, 2026 — a detention that has since ignited a global debate about two-tier policing in Britain.

**What happened at Rangrez:**
Kapoor, whose 16-year-old restaurant displayed a sign reading 'Proudly we don't sell Halal,' had faced months of harassment after publicly committing to serve only jhatka meat in keeping with his Sikh faith. Crowds numbering between dozens and over a hundred gathered outside Rangrez on March 13 and 14, blocking the entrance and chanting slogans. Police arrived, and officers arrested Kapoor — not the demonstrators — reportedly because he was carrying his kirpan, a ceremonial blade that UK law permits Sikhs to carry as a religious article of faith. He was released without charge.

**The discrimination allegation:**
After his release, Kapoor publicly charged the Met with 'negligence, harassment, and false arrest,' stating: 'The Met Police refused to help us and failed us on many occasions.' His wife, Khushi, directly named Mayor Sadiq Khan, accusing him of instructing police to protect one community over another — allegations Khan's office has not publicly addressed. The Metropolitan Police told LBC they could not clarify the circumstances of the arrest or confirm whether any charges were filed. Kapoor also cited a pattern of inaction stretching back over two years, including death and rape threats against his family that police reportedly dismissed.

**What to watch next:**
Whether Kapoor formally files a civil discrimination suit in British courts will determine whether this controversy moves from a social media flashpoint into a legal reckoning for London's police accountability framework.

nri_angle: For Indian-Americans watching Britain's multicultural experiment closely, Kapoor's case raises an uncomfortable question that resonates here too: whether South Asian minority communities — Sikh and Hindu — receive equal police protection in Western cities that claim to champion religious pluralism.
